utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am sorry that technical problems with the videolink have caused a delay in the start of today's proceedings. We are now ready. Mrs. Tuma, you are to take the witness. Is that so? Thank you. If the court staff could make the connection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you be kind enough to take the card that is given to you by the court officer and read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll doing it without reading the affirmation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mrs. Tuma will be asking you some questions. She will commence now. Thank you. Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, do you hear me? So I have contact with you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And my name is Marie Tuma, and I am a trial attorney here for the Office of the Prosecutor, and I will do the examination-in-chief and put some questions to you. I hope that you are comfortable there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Dosen, I would like you to tell us your personal background, if you were married and to whom. We can start there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: My name is Ljubica Dosen. I'm married to Martin Dosen, a Croat defender who went missing in the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When did you marry? When was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Back in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And did that marriage bring any children?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Tanja Dosen, our daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when was she born?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And where were you living with your family?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: In Vukovar, Mose Pijade Street, as well as at Olajnica, 12/24. That's all in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Where did you have your family house? On which address was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Our home was in Mose Pijade Street, number 32, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And then you mentioned another address as well. What was that referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's a flat at Olajnica in Vukovar. 12/24, third floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And during the marriage, what kind of living did you do? What kind of -- how -- in what way did you earn the money to live upon?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was working at Borovo, the factory. I had been working there for 20 years, in fact. But then my husband became a professional fisherman, and we opened a restaurant on the banks of the Danube. I cooked the fish, and we had plenty of guests in the summer. We sold our own fish there, the fish that my husband would catch in the Danube. That's what he did. He was a professional fisherman.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And your husband's name, what is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Martin Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Where were he coming from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: He is a native of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did he have any siblings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. He had two brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you please name the brothers, the name of the brothers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Tadija Dosen was his elder brother and Ivan Dosen as his younger brother. His sister's was Ilica Dosen, and the other sister's name Marija Dosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was your husband ever involved in any kind of political activities as far as your recollection is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: My husband was never involved in politics in any way. He was never a member of any political organisation or anything like that until the commotion in Vukovar began. It was at this point that he joined the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when was that? Can you tell us that if you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: That was -- I can't remember exactly, but it may have been in April or May 1990, thereabouts, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In terms of his being as a member of the HDZ party, did he take any actions in terms of his membership?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Well, he was a party member. He was not a member of any of their boards or the presidency. He was simply an HDZ member, which he believed to be a good thing. He agreed with what they were saying. He was a sympathiser, a political sympathiser. It was that simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were you at any point when your husband so to say were dealing or supporting of the HDZ party, did you have the chance or the possibilities to get to know the members of that party through their faces or through their names?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was not a member of the HDZ myself, or any other political party for that matter. I did not know who their president was at the time, or where they met, or if they had any meetings, in fact. I was mostly dealing with our family. I looked after our children, and I was never involved in politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when did the conflict, the armed conflict started, around?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The way I see things, it all began in May in Borovo Selo when the attack occurred against the Croatian police officers. It was then that the quarrels began as well as the separation. There was a mass exodus of the Serb population from Vukovar, and one could clearly feel, as early as then, that something wasn't right and that people were starting to go their own ways. Up until this point in time, we had been managing to have proper friendly relations. Most of my friends, as a matter of fact, were Serbs more than Croats. We didn't really believe this to be that important, but at this point in time, one clearly had the feeling that something would not be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You have mentioned here May, can you clarify what year you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was not physically present in Borovo Selo myself. Those were stories and rumours that I heard. People were saying that a rebellion had broken out there, the so-called log revolution. They said it was no longer possible to go there, and they sent a team of Croatian police officers to check what was going on. Based on what others were telling me at the time, a massacre occurred there. They killed a number of our lads, just because they were not the same ethnic group as them. They were from the police force. Now we call it the MUP, the M-U-P, and they wouldn't have any of those chequer-boards, the symbol that they wore on their caps, and that's why they committed this massacre and slew those lads over there. I wasn't there myself personally, but I know that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What year was it? You mentioned the month May. What year is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: May 1990 -- 1991. I think -- I think it was 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Dosen, Martin Dosen, take any actions himself when there was an ongoing conflict, armed conflict ongoing in the area of Vukovar? You mentioned earlier here that you presented him as a Croat defender. When was that when he became a Croat defender?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: When the whole thing began, up until August 1990, we had been managing to get on with our lives in Vukovar, in a manner of speaking. But then what we started noticing is that in the surrounding areas, on the outskirts, in the villages of Brsadin and other villages, you could no longer access those areas. And then in Vukovar people started organising, setting up some sort of guard duty so that they could not approach from the Danube or from those villages and reach the centre of town. Serbs where beginning to leave Vukovar en masse and most of those staying behind were Croats. Their wives and children would also stay behind, and that was the worst thing, only the men had gone. And then the shelling and the firing began, and we suddenly understood that this would lead to no good. But there was no way out at this point. We had to adapt and try to get on with our lives because there was no way out. The only way out would have been across those villages because at this point in time, we were encircled.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, I asked you the question if you remember when Mr. Dosen got to be a Croat defender. You mention here August 1990. Can we be -- agree that it must have been the year 1991 instead? It's sort of the common knowledge here.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, what I meant was 1991, because in August 1991 my husband was wounded by a shell. Of course, he was on his way to get some food in one of our department stores. He was hit by a piece of shrapnel in the leg and he was hospitalised. I'm sorry for saying 1990. 1991 was the year I had in mind. It was in August 1991 that he returned back home. And then he said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for that please. We will take that further on when it comes to if and when he was wounded. But we can agree upon that it was the year 1991. And you talked, you said here that Martin Dosen here was involved as a Croat defender. What was he doing as a Croat defender?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What was he doing as a Croat defender? Was he engaged in something special as a Croat defender at the time in August 1991 and further on during the autumn 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was in autumn [as interpreted] 1991 that he joined in actively. But then the shelling began, this is something that I need to explain, that a lot of shops were damage. There was no water or electricity by this time, and he joined forces with his fellow fighters and friends in order to collect whatever food was left in those shops as well as items of clothing and candles for lighting. They all gathered at one place and these things were distributed to Vukovar's residents, those who were in need. He was a member of the staff that was in charge of the supplies of the town of Vukovar. The women, children and men, everybody, they were told to come to the Nama department store so that they could be given food, medicines, candles, whatever. Because at this point in time we had run out of water, electricity, and all we had on a daily basis was non-stop shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry for interrupting but there is one thing in the transcript on page 7, line 3. I think the witness said that her husband joined in actively in August 1991 and what the transcript says is autumn 1991. I think there's an error there; it's probably a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If could you sort that out, please, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, we need to have one more -- an answer from you in order clarify some translation issues here in courtroom. So one more time I'm asking you, when did your husband Martin Dosen became actively joined the Croat defenders in 1991? Can you give us a more clear answer there, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: August 1991. I would consider that to be autumn.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. Now that is clarified. So from August 1991, he was a member, so to say, or active as a Croat defender. And you mention here that the city was run out of water. Were there any other possibilities to have access to water than by through the normal ways, so to say? Did you have that in Vukovar? And was there a possibility for the people to get hold of water or were they in difficulties in that sense? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: You could go to privates home because some of the private homes had wells in their gardens. Arctic wells. And some of us who were living in those residential buildings would go there to fetch water. But in order to reach those houses, you had to cross a large clearing, but they found out soon enough that people were crossing that clearing in a bid to fetch water for their household, so they started shelling the clearing and many people were hit on their way to fetch water.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. How do you know that, that they were hit by shelling while trying to get hold of water through those wells?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: My building at Olajnica was number 12 and that is across the way from Kidriceva Street where those houses were. You could see it from your window, and we knew anyway. I was one of those people who had to cross that area in order to get water. You couldn't go on without water. You have to use your water-closet, you have to wash. We are women after all, aren't we? We needed water. We needed water for food as well, and for washing. We simply had no choice but to go there. We couldn't go to the loo, we couldn't go outside, and the shelling was constant from early in the morning to late in the evening, and you couldn't leave your building for a second because the shelling was so heavy. That should give you an idea what life was like for us in those buildings. We had no cellars, no windows, and hardly any doors at all, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, what time-frame are you talking about now when you're describing this situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time period between August and November, those four or three months. Those months were sheer hell. None of those who were not there could even begin to imagine what it was like. Could even begin to imagine that somebody could do a thing like that. Uninterrupted shelling for three months. That was pure hell. I wouldn't wish that upon anyone, especially when winter was upon us, with November encroaching and the cold, can you believe what it was like for those women?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I understand, Mrs. Dosen. I would like you to answer directly my questions. So how did you know that people were shelled or hit by shellings when they were trying to reach water out of the wells? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And how many times did you see that? Was it once or was it often? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what are you talking about that in terms of numbers? Can you give us some kind of assessment in that sense, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Well, about 20 times, at least. I'm positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So about --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I personally witnessed this shelling at least about 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And then you -- is it that those 20 times between in the period of August to November 1991, or is it another time-frame when you are -- when you did observe about around 20 times personally that people were shelled when fetching water from the wells?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: That is between August and November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The well sites, were they well-known around for people in Vukovar? Can you describe something about that for us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Well, we communicated with each other, and if there was one person who knew about one such well, they would share this with other people, and then these other people would share this with somebody else. We tried to help each other out. Everybody needed help, so we passed information on to other people; and conversely, we would be told by other people, there is a well over there in that house, so we would go there to get some water. We went like that several times, but then two persons were injured, and later on we were too scared to continue going there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. How long were you able to stay in your house, your family house, during the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: We stayed on in the house throughout August and for the first half of September. At this point my husband said that we could no longer stay there. He went to do his guard duty at night in the Nama department store, so Tanja and I stayed back alone. He told us that we would be better off and safer at the Olajnica because there were more people there and more women. He said his mind would be more at ease if we stayed at Olajnica instead with more people around so that he at least knew that we were not on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And did you go there? Did you move to another location then according to your husband, your late husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Then Tanja and myself went to Olajnica and we stayed there until the end, just before going to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was in mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And for what reason did you go to the hospital in mid-September?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Mid-September, no, that's not when we left for the hospital. We went to Olajnica in mid-September. And we went to the hospital on the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And before we move into that area on the 17th November, were your husband ever injured during the armed conflict? And when and for what then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: My husband was wounded in August 1991, by a shrapnel. As I said, he went to the department store and to the Territorial Defence's offices. He wanted to come by some food and to see how was distributed. The second time he was wounded in his right upper arm. He heard that his brother's son was killed on the street, and he tried to move him out and that's when he was shot in the arm. He went to the hospital, and they immobilised his arm without any surgery and he was sent home and that's when he joined us at Olajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, you have mentioned two times that your husband was injured during the armed conflict. Were there any other times that he was injured after those two times that you have recently described?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 16th of November in the morning. Our building was set on fire, and a number of children and women remained in the building. He tried to save them, and he kept saying that everyone should leave the building because it was on fire. I came out together with Tanja and my sister's son in my arms. Martin remained in our apartment, because in the apartment next to ours there was an old lady who couldn't leave by herself. He was trying to help her. She managed to get out of the building, but he no longer had the time to come out. There was a lot of smoke and fire by that time, so he stayed outside on the balcony. We yelled from the street to try to run down the burning stairs. I don't know exactly what happened, perhaps he was panicking, he was wounded by that time, and they tried to throw a rope to him, to the balcony so that he could try and use it to lower himself from the third floor. But since he was quite a stout man, and he was using only his left arm, and he must have ran out of strength. Therefore, he let go of the rope and hit the concrete. His spine was hurt and was paralysed in his upper body. Then I asked the people who were there to transfer him to the hospital by any which means.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what day was this, Mrs. Dosen, that he was transported to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was on the 16th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you accompany him at that time, or was it later on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't accompany him, because my daughter was crying hysterically, and I stayed with her. The shelling went on irrespective of the things taking place. We couldn't go but, rather, the guys who knew the way went. They carried him on the stretcher because each building had its stretcher, and that's how he was carried to the hospital. Tanja and myself did not accompany him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Do you remember, I know it's difficult sometimes while it's long time ago, but do you happen to remember what day you went then to the hospital? And did you go there alone or accompanied with someone else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: On the 17th, during the night two guys came from the hospital. They woke me up as well as Tanja in the building. We were told to pack our stuff, that Martin sent for us so that we could reach the hospital. There was a convoy to be put together to evacuate those wounded, as well as the women and children from Vukovar, because the situation was becoming unbearable. We tried to tell all those who wanted to go to the hospital, and a column was formed. It was during the night, and I remember that it was pouring rain. There was still shelling and one could hear tanks approaching the city. Martin probably knew that they were to enter the city soon, and he sent for us to come to the hospital. There were around 20 women and children in that column.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Dosen, if I understand you right, during the night to the 18th you were wakened up and you were transported --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was it during the 17th and the 18th, if I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was on the 17th, during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And how was it then when you came to the hospital? Can you give us a picture, briefly, about the overall situation? We have heard it from other witnesses as well, so you don't need to go into details. Did you meet your husband in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: When we reached the hospital Martin's sister-in-law was there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, mother-in-law was there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: As well as his sister-in-law's two children because his sister-in-law was previously killed, and we were all part of the same column. As soon as I entered the hospital, I saw my husband right away, because his bed was right next to the door. We greeted each other, and then we were asked to go to the first floor, because we were not allowed to stay with the wounded. They were not in any hospital rooms. They were in a cellar that was emptied previously and beds were put next to each other. Those were not regular hospital rooms but, rather, corridors filled with wounded people and the beds were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. You earlier described here that your husband, he fell from the third floor, and he was brought to hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, could we interrupt a moment, please? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction for the transcript. Perhaps we could clarify this with the witness. I thought I heard in B/C/S that the witness said when they came to the hospital on page 14, line 4, she mentioned that apart from her mother-in-law and the late Martin's sister's children, there were also Tanja and Martin's younger brother, Ivan, and that did not enter the transcript. Perhaps we could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, we need to have some clarification here and it's only in terms of the transcript, so it's not according to your answers, earlier answers, so to say, so we get the translation right here. So you were telling us here when you reached the hospital. Who else you said that you met, you saw your husband Martin Dosen, and you also mentioned relatives of yours, your family that were in the hospital when you got there. Can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. The way I understood, and perhaps the witness could clarify, that together with her there were those relatives who came to the hospital at that time. Perhaps we shouldn't lead the witness in that but let the witness clarify who was within that group that came to the hospital with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, once again, I'm sorry for this, but can you please clarify who was in the group that came to the hospital when it comes to your relatives? You mentioned a group of people earlier. Can you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. My daughter, Tanja Dosen, was with me, my mother [as interpreted], Marija Dosen, his brother Ivan Dosen, and two of their late sister's children were there. She had been killed in October 1991, and the two children were under age. Their names were Jelena and Igor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like you to describe the injuries that your husband received by the fall from the third floor. You said that he was hospitalised. Were there any doctor who examined him? Were you getting any kind of information or explanation what kind of injuries he was suffering from due to that fall? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: When I came to the hospital, the first thing I did was to speak with Martin. That is my husband. And he told me that he was examined by Dr. Njavro, and another doctor whose name I can't recall. Perhaps it is not so important. They told him that his spine was injured, that his vertebrae, his first, second, third and fourth vertebrae were injured. But that, having in mind the situation at the Vukovar Hospital, they were unable to provide any assistance for him. The only thing they could do was provide some pain relief and tranquilizers. They suggested that all of his documentation be taken to Zagreb or wherever it was that he would go from Vukovar to continue with treatment. The thing is that he couldn't lift his upper body. His head -- his head would fall backwards and he couldn't sit up. So practically speaking, he couldn't move. He was paralysed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. And when you were there in that scenery when you came to the hospital, you met your husband there, there were relatives, what kind of observations did you do otherwise? What kind of people were located in the hospital when you were there, when you entered the hospital during that night?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: When I arrived that night there were lots of civilians in the hospital coming from all directions within the city. Not only from Olajnica, but from other parts. All those who had heard that a convoy would be formed, they came to the hospital. And it was overcrowded, it just couldn't hold so many people. Dr. Bosanac asked that we all go to the first floor so as not to disturb the wounded. Since my husband couldn't move, I asked Dr. Njavro to allow me to see him and to stay with him. Hence I was allowed to do that, and I was seated on his bed. He told me then that his brother Tadija was wounded and that he was in the hospital as well. And that his sister's son was wounded as well and was in the hospital too. And then I left to see the two men. I wanted to see what their shape, what shape they were in. Because they were not with us in the building during the shelling. They were in another part of town. It is then that I saw Martin Jakubovski and Tadija. Both of them were wounded at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did they have? Were you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Martin Jakubovski, the nephew, was hit by a rifle grenade in his right hand. The hand was fixated with screws, and his pelvis was injured. As for the brother-in-law, a shell entered their shelter and he suffered internal injuries inside his chest and he had some bruising on his cheek.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: If I understood you right, Mrs. Dosen, you mentioned here also the brother, Tadija, that he was also injured. Was that right for me to understand your saying that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And did you see his injuries?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what did they consist of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Tadija had a rather long cut on his cheek and had a Band-Aid on his chest. I couldn't see the actual injuries, but it seemed that he was injured in the chest by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. You mentioned here earlier also the other brother, Ivan Dosen. Did you meet him in the hospital? If so, did you see him, if he did have any injuries and what kind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. Ivan came with us from Olajnica. He came to the hospital as a civilian. He wasn't wounded. He simply came as part of the group to be with the children and with us, because he was the only male in the family who was present. We later on had to send some other guys for Tadija's wife and daughter. They were in a different building, close to the Danube, in the cellar. We were afraid that they would be caught in those cellars. Therefore, during the night two guys went out and brought them into the hospital and then they joined us.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The next day what did you -- were you with your husband during that day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And did you -- what kind of people did you see around him or in the hospital at that point when you -- on the next day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: All those around him in the hospital were wounded. I knew some of them, I didn't some other [as interpreted]. I had some cigarettes with me, and we baked some bread and I brought them that. They were in a miserable state. Before the war they probably weighed 80 to 100 kilos each and now they were starved, neglected, and one could smell blood. There was nothing much for them to be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: We couldn't give them anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. Did you see any soldiers around in the hospital, or outside the hospital at any point of time during that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: On that day, the 17th, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The next day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: On the 18th, that is the next day, I went out and I saw Mr. Bilic, aka Bili, and Dr. Bosanac. I saw them talking to a -- to some military officers and that they were being taken away. I returned immediately. I sat on my husband's bed, and I told him, "Martin, I don't know what is happening, but Dr. Bosanac was taken away by the military, and I don't know what will happen next." Later on that evening, talking to some other people and through rumours, we learned that Dr. Bosanac went to negotiate the military, so that Vukovar would be surrendered to their hands as well as the hospital. And she demanded that the wounded and civilians be taken out on a convoy out of Vukovar and that there be no massacre. We all awaited what would come next and what sort of a deal Dr. Bosanac would manage to put together.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, I -- going back to my question: Did you see any soldiers? You were mentioning here that Bosanac was taken away, et cetera. But in and around the hospital, did you see any presence of soldiers on this day where -- that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not at that time. There were some people treated in the hospital. There were three soldiers there who had been wounded. They were hospitalised inside the Vukovar Hospital. They were there together with our wounded. They were provided medical assistance, the same way it was provided to our wounded people. Nobody refused to give assistance. They were simply there, and apart from the three, there were no other soldiers inside or outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were the hospital at any time surrounded by soldiers? And when was that then, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I can't be certain as to the date. It may have been between the 18th and the 19th, during the night. In any case, I went outside and I saw the military there. It was dark and I couldn't see what sort of military, but I could see heavy weaponry being placed around the hospital. In the meantime, I believe it was on the 18th, two officers came in, because they came to fetch the three wounded soldiers who were in the hospital. They came to get them. They told them to leave the hospital, but the soldiers told them that they were fine where they were, that they were treated fairly. However, they used force to take all of -- all of them outside. And then they put a soldier at the entrance of the hospital so that no one could leave any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, here you said that you were not certain about the date, if it was the 18th or 19th November that you went outside and that you saw heavy weaponry outside the hospital, but you did not know what kind of military --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... When you say "heavy weaponry," what does that mean? What did you see in terms of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: When I came out I could see -- I could see tank barrels turned towards the hospital. I can't tell you exactly what sort of weaponry it was. I only can presume that they were tanks or heavy weaponry with their barrels turned to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. You also mention here there were two officer who came in in order to fetch the three soldiers you're talking about. What kind of officers were they? Can you describe what kind of army they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Regular JNA soldiers and officers. I can't say for certain, but when they came Dr. Bosanac had already returned, and by that time we knew that the hospital was to be evacuated. There were two JNA officers who went to see the three soldiers directly. I was seated on my husband's bed at the time, and I said, Ah, it seems we are now getting cigarettes and food, because the liberators are here. One of the officer hit himself on the chest, he said that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, he tried his pockets.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: And he said, "I apologise, missus, but I don't seem to have any cigarettes on me, or food either," and he continued on towards the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned here JNA officers. Can you distinguish a JNA officer from another officer, so to say? Do you know that for sure?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can be certain of that, because my first husband was a JNA officer. I know the difference between the star and the four Ss, and the cockade. I have seen all three before.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. Did you see any of other kind of military in or around the hospital at the time where we are talking about, and that was the next day after you entered into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Well, the night before the evacuation, the night between the 19th and the 20th, I left the hospital again to stand there with the wounded. It was morning already. I went outside, believing that nobody would harm me. Why wouldn't I, after all, I was thinking to myself. I'm not a prisoner, am I? However, when I looked up I saw a good friend of Martin's. I can tell you about his insignia. He was wearing a pure Chetnik uniform with a Chetnik insignia. He had a magazine slung over his shoulder. He was just there. On your way to the hospital, you have to walk up a slope and he was standing up there with his fists closed, shouting, "Serbia, Serbia," and I went back to see Martin to tell him that his friend was there and to say nothing about it. However, I was followed by this friend of Martin's into the room. I heard them call him Capalo. Martin looked at him and said, "Capalo, for God's sake, what sort of uniform is it that you're wearing?" And Capalo just told him to keep his trap shut. He said, "This is a Chetnik uniform. I told you this would all be Serbia, didn't I?" Martin just placed his hand over his eyes and averted his gaze. He was no longer in the mood to talk to him. I spoke to the man and said, "This isn't Serbia. I don't believe it will ever be." And then he turned to face me and told me, "You and I will have this discussion somewhere else." And then Martin told me, "Please say no more. Don't talk to him ever again." He was one of those who were wearing pure Chetnik uniforms, but then the reservists started streaming in, and their uniforms were again different.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was made out of a special rough cloth. They did not have the five-pointed star but, rather, they had the four Ss.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, can you describe for us the differences in your point of view, between the -- as you said Chetnik insignia and reservists. What kind of uniforms were they wearing in order to be distinguished from each other when you saw that in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The distinction is that the Chetnik uniforms, and I'm referring to those people wearing proper pure Chetnik uniforms, those people were wearing fur caps with cockades, and they would have two cartridge belts strapped across their chest and automatic rifles as well. The reservists, on the other hand, were wearing helmets, and on the helmet they had the four Ss sign. But sort of hand-painted. You could tell the difference from the JNA soldiers who had proper JNA uniforms with a five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. Did you see any other -- you just mentioned the name Capalo here. Did you see any other in the same outfit, so to say, the same category in or around the hospital at the time? Chetniks, I said, or reservists.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I can tell you that I only saw one or two Chetniks wearing the same sort of uniform that Capalo was wearing. I can't say that there were more of them, because there weren't. There were many more reservists, some locals, people I knew, and some young men as well. You could see that those were fresh conscripts who had probably received some sort of abbreviated training and were forced to go to Vukovar. Those were no regular forces. You could clearly see that they were reservists who had been called up and forced to go to war. I can tell you that there were quite many very young men or boys among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. I heard here that you a couple of times at least were outside the hospital during the night-time. Did you see any kind of activities that you did find remarkable, so to say, during the nights that you spent in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: One thing that I believe to be the -- more noteworthy than anything else that was going on at the time was the fact that they brought back Dr. Bosanac. They had her isolated in a room which meant that she was no longer able to communicate with the patients. Frankly, all of the reservists, all locals from Vukovar who decided to be a member of -- be members of the reserve forces, the JNA no longer allowed those people to mingle with the wounded carrying their weapons. But it was all fine for as long as the regular army were still there. However, during the next night they left, and this was when our lads starting disappearing, those -- those of them who were in the hospital. And we didn't see them again. On whose orders and why were their names called, I don't know. The fact is, they led them away, they led them outside, and we never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, I would like to stay a bit -- we were talking here about when the JNA left, that our -- as you mentioned here, our lads were disappearing, and they were called out and led -- taken out. Can you explain what happened? Did you see this, and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: All I can say is they got in, two of them, three of them, reservists, and they would say, "You, come with us. We need you. And you too, come with us." And they would just lead these people away from that room in which we were staying. I don't know what happened later or where these people were taken to. I can't say for sure because I didn't see this myself. What I can say is that these people did not return.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you see any people, as you mention here, were led away? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Because those among us who were at the hospital and who believed that they would leave with the convoy, there were a lot of defenders who were no longer able to leave town. They had to either turn over their weapons or surrender, but those people from Vukovar whom they knew were standing with the JNA outside the hospital sharing names with them, sharing the names of those people who were inside the hospital whom they knew, and then they would go into the hospital and get those people. So these names had to be shared by people from Vukovar who knew these people. I don't believe any JNA officer from outside would have been able to identify these people. There had to be someone with them who was a source of local knowledge to share these names.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, you mention here the term "people." Can you expand that a little, what you mean by "people"? People that were led away.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Young men who had stood guard around town in the suburbs, like my husband. They came to the hospital to be there and wait for the convoy. They were all defenders in their opinion, just like all the wounded were, the way they saw it. I believe over a thousand of those people must have been wound by shells and not in combat. There wasn't much combat inside the town itself. There was just a lot of killing of innocent people. There were a lot of Croat and Serb civilians who had been wounded. I'm certain that those people were not wounded by Croats; rather, they were being wounded by shells on account of the constant shelling. There was no combat, hand-to-hand combat in the town itself. And nobody can tell me that there was, because I was there myself. I know that there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, I didn't ask you about that, and I do want to -- you to realise and think of that answer to my questions, please. And you mention here that it was young men when you described the people who were led out of the hospital. And were there any -- did those young men, did they have anything in common?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The only distinguishing feature was that they were looking for shelter, if you ask me, inside the hospital. They were looking for a place to hide, fearing that there would be acts of vengeance, but I find it very difficult to say. I knew some of them. For example the plaster technician, Marko, went missing overnight. He disappeared from the hospital and we never saw him again. There were many young men I knew from Vukovar, but I didn't know their names. Lots of them disappeared and never came back. I don't know all of their names, but I did know many of them by sight. We would meet in the streets of Vukovar, but I was not the same age as them, so I didn't know their names. They just selected certain people and they probably knew why they chose some people and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, I would like to stop here for a while, and you say that they selected certain people. Who were "they"? Who did do the selection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. It was like this: Two reservists would come in and say, "You, you come with us. You come with us too, and you too. We need you for something. Come with us." I have no idea on whose orders they were acting. There was nothing going on in the same room where the wounded were. This was all taking place somewhere outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, thank you. You mentioned also that there were locals who shared names with the JNA, at least you assumed that, if I understand you right. Do you know -- happen to know who those locals were who shared names with the JNA? Now we're talking about, as you say, those people that were led out of the hospital in the night-time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. All those who left Vukovar were reservists. But none of them were willing to come forward and say, "I'm the one, I'm wearing this uniform." They just stood back and they provided the names and then they would send somebody else, those reservists who arrived from Kraljevo or Valjevo, or someplace like that. They just didn't know. All they knew were their names, and that's why they called out the names and took the people away but not a single one was willing to show their face, come forward and say, "I'm the one. I gave the names away."

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. How many did you see were led away in this way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The evening, when I was with Martin, they took away about four or five of them, including Marko, the plaster technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Who was -- Mrs. Dosen, who was Marko, what -- was he a normal guy, so to say, or was he in any way active during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I knew him as Marko, the plaster technician. He was actually working at the hospital as a paramedic. He helped with the plaster-casts. What they called Croat defenders came to the hospital, and I suppose they tried -- well, I guess Dr. Bosanac must have allowed this, must have known about this. They tried to save them somehow, and they would apply plaster-casts on perfectly healthy limbs, so as to make it seem as if these people too were wounded in order to avoid them being taken away by force, biding their time until the convoy arrived so that they could all be evacuated. However, when the army got into the hospital, somebody told them about this and then they took several of those away, several of those people who had these plaster-casts on top of healthy limbs. They realised that these people were not wounded in any way, and it was probably on account of this that they took Marko, the plaster technician, away so that they could ask him questions about why he had done this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. You just -- you earlier you mentioned that Martin Dosen he was injured, et cetera. And do you know if there were any medical records written concerning his injuries and his treatment in the hospital? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you see that? Did you see the medical records?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what happened with those medical records? Were they in the hospital or were they -- where were they ended up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Well, the next morning the evacuation of the wounded was supposed to take place, and then Nurse Biba placed patients' case histories and temperature charts in a plastic bag next to each of the patients. And the assumption was that this would later be used to treat these people once they'd been evacuated. So each of the patients were given their own case histories wrapped up in a plastic bag, in a small plastic bag. I was still perched on my husband's bed, so I took the little plastic bag with his case history and that's why I had them on me when I came to Zagreb, because I was later separated from my husband and the documents stayed with me. I'm still in possession of the originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. We'll go through that later on more in detail when it comes to the medical records of your husband. And how -- when you -- where did you spend the last night in the hospital? That is, the night before the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: On my husband's bed, where his feet were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what was his condition at that time? Medical condition.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Whoever knows my husband knows that he was a good athlete. He was a professional fisherman, he was an active person. He couldn't reconcile himself to being unable to move for the rest of his life, so he spent a great deal of his time just sobbing.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was he able to walk during that night? Was he still immobile?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, he certainly wasn't able to move about. He was entirely immobile. He was unable to move his body in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Then the next morning, now we're on the 20th November, what happened then in the morning? You said here that you spent the night by your husband. And what happened then in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The next morning we were surprised to see two soldiers at the door. They had some sort of a list and they started calling names out from that list. I was surprised, because they started calling out the names of Martin Dosen, Tadija Dosen, Ivan Dosen, Martin Jakubovski. We were surprised that they started calling out individual names. I asked the nurse if this was the beginning of the evacuation, and she said, "Yes, we need to put your husband on a stretcher, since he can't move. We'll have to carry him." And then Martin said, "Ljubica, just one thing, where is Tanja? Please, don't leave me. Stay with me throughout." So when the nurses lifted him off the bed and put him on a stretcher, Tanja and I followed his stretcher. But then the turmoil began inside the hospital, and those of the wounded who could still move just headed for the exit because they had been told to start leaving the hospital because the convoy was there and the evacuation would soon commence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. I would like to take it in sequence, so to say. But thank you so much. You said here that in the morning there were two soldiers at the entrance, if I remember it right now and that they were having a list. What kind of soldiers were they? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Those were reservists.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what happened? You said there were two soldiers, they were having this list. Were there any other military person in the -- close by, or were those two reservists isolated, so to say, when they were arriving with that list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: They were those two soldiers standing on their own with the list. But as soon as we went outside, and I followed my husband, we found ourselves facing a gauntlet made up of soldiers on either side. The wounded walked up, and those of us who were civilians, and I was walking along next to my husband's stretcher, were searched and we had to hand over any items that we had on us. A pair of scissors, a pocket-knife, pieces of jewellery, that sort of thing. Our bags were searched. I managed somehow to get past them, as I was trying to follow my husband's stretcher. But as you were passing by, the first thing that struck me as strange was that we weren't taking the hospital's principal entrance but, rather, the back exit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here, Mrs. Dosen. I would like to just take in sequences, otherwise I have to go back. So please just answer my questions. So close to the two soldiers, as you mentioned, was reservists. They were isolated, so to say, if I understood you right.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And there were other soldiers standing outside who were searching people and who formed a gauntlet on the way out. There were various kinds of soldiers standing outside, those wearing camouflage uniforms, reservists, JNA soldiers, officers. It was a mixture of soldiers, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When it comes to that list, did those two soldiers have that list in their hands? Or one of the soldiers perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. One of them. And he was reading from the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what was he reading from the list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The names of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And do you today remember the names on that list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I remember the first names from the list. Because I left the room soon after my husband Martin was among the first to be taken away. He was the first name on that list, so they took him away, and I followed. I don't know -- I don't know about the rest of the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Do you remember any other names on that list that was called out? You mention here your husband's name, that he was on the list. Do you remember any other names on that list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Both of his brothers, Tadija Dosen, Ivan Dosen, little Marko Jakubovski Dosen. When I realised that all of them were being called out, it struck me as strange or suspicious that their names topped the list. I thought that was some sort of a record of the wounded who were inside the hospital, but I'm afraid that that, after all, might not have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned now a few names here, Mrs. Dosen. And you also said earlier that you didn't remember all the names of that list. Do you today remember about how many names were called out from that specific list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may be too early objecting, but I believe the witness said that her husband was among the first and that she followed him outside soon after. I think the OTP's asking a little too much. I believe this to be a leading question, but I may have been slightly overzealous, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not a leading question at all. It's asking does she know, and if your understanding is correct, she won't know. But if she does know, we'll need to learn how she knows. Please carry on, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Those names, Mrs. Dosen, on that specific list that were called out, you mentioned a couple of names here. How did you know that those names were on the list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Well, if you're holding a piece of paper in your hand and reading from it, and names are being called out, well, then, it must be a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you hear this when the names were called out, Mrs. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. You have just described the list and you described also specific names on that list and also other names that you don't really know about. How -- can you today give us a kind of estimation how many names, about, could be in total on that specific list that were read out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I was able to hear about 10 names off that list prior to my husband being put on the stretcher and he being moved out towards the exit. After that I could no longer hear who was being called out, but the wounded came out of the hospital in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay, Mrs. Dosen. I just -- you said about 10 names you heard from that list. Were there any kind of characteristics concerning those 10 names that were called out that you heard was called out, that were in common from those 10 names? Do you remember that, Mrs. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: To my mind, and at least at the moment when all of this was taking place, and one needs to bear in mind that I was under severe stress and I just wanted things to start moving, at that time it appeared suspicious that those were all members of my family and friends of ours, Martin's cousins. It means that somebody must have singled them out, out of all those people. To have so many members of our family and so many of our men to be singled out, to my mind, that was quite suspicious.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, you named -- you mention here that it seems to be that they were singled out, the male family members and also Martin Dosen's cousins. Did they have anything else in common than to be relatives?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. Perhaps in their view they were defending their families and they may have heard that they had carried arms. My husband had a gun, a pistol, as well as a Kalashnikov. But he had that in order to protect his family and not to kill anyone. I don't know what other characteristics they may have had in common, apart from being HDZ members, and being the people who tried to put together a system of defence of the city to protect the children and women of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Because there were very few men in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, we're going to take a break now so hat you can have a free time for about 20 minutes and then we will continue. So we will now adjourn and resume at a quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma will now continue her questioning. Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, you mentioned, I'm talking about the list now, only the list and nothing else. You mentioned three names that were called out from that specific list. And that was Ivan Dosen, Tadija Dosen and little, as you mentioned here, Martin Jakubovski. Were there any other names that you remember today from that list, that were called out, together with those three individuals?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Zvonko Vulic was called out, Ivan Ahmetovic as well, Ivan Vulic. I think that's that as far as I can remember. I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And when you mentioned, if I understood you right now because I don't have the transcript right in front of me concerning those names that you heard were called out, was it Martin Jakubovski that was called out? Is that the same person as little Marko? So we do have it this clear here, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No. Martin Jakubovski is my husband's sister's son.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Was he called out from that list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: These people that you just mentioned now by name that were called out from that specific list, have you ever seen them since then, since that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And do you happen to know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Ivan Ahmetovic, his body was exhumed at Ovcara. Martin Jakubovski was exhumed at Ovcara as well. And nothing -- no information exists for the remaining people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And how about your husband, he was also on that list?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. He was the first one on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Any information about him that you have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: When I came to Zagreb, a friend of his called on me. He was from Vukovar but had left to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, you said here --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Since Martin was a good friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here, Mrs. Dosen. You said here that Ivan Dosen was exhumed in Ovcara. What happened to your husband, Martin Dosen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: No, not Ivan. Not Ivan Dosen, but Ivan Ahmetovic was exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: My husband is still missing. Allegedly he was killed in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. I will leave the sequence, if I may say so, with the list. And I want you to go back now in your memory and just take step by step and answer my questions and not talk more than I'm asking after. So you were -- where were you standing when the soldier, as you referred to earlier, was calling out the names from that list? Where were you at that point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Next to my husband's bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And where was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: In the hospital, in the room where all the wounded were. Martin's bed was right next to the door, as one was leaving the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what did -- what happened exactly after that? You was by your husband's bed. Were you there all the time or were there any kind of transport?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: As I stood next to the bed, two nurses came, because my husband needed to be taken from the bed to be put on the stretcher, as he couldn't walk. But they were unable to put him on the stretcher because he was too heavy for them, and then two soldiers came in and they carried his stretcher. Tanja and myself walked next to the stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did those two soldiers, as you just mentioned now, they should carry him on the stretcher, were they anyone who directed them to do that, or did they do that on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very leading question. I wish to remind that the witness has answered to this question several times before that. On page 31, line 14, she said that two soldiers came and she clearly stated that she saw the additional soldiers and officers only after having left the building. And she clearly stated that in -- on page 33, line 20. And now again the Prosecutor, in the leading way, wishes to receive a certain type of answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I quite agree with your recollection about her earlier evidence, but when asked about what happened by the husband's bed, without any suggestion of soldiers from Mrs. Tuma it was the witness who said what happened was two nurses came, put him on a stretcher, he was too heavy, two soldiers came. That was entirely the evidence of the witness without any prompting about soldiers. And the further question then of Mrs. Tuma was merely whether they came on their on their own initiative or did someone else order or direct them. I don't see that as an improper question, given that there has been the specific mention by the witness of two soldiers. Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, could you please answer that question, and if you don't remember it, I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I do remember it. They were probably ordered to come and help carry him. The two must have been aware that they were far too fragile to carry him on a stretcher. They must have received an order to assist, as the nurses were unable to. As soon as his name was called out, he was supposed to be evacuated from the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, I need to know what you saw and observed. I don't want to have "probably," so to say. You are here to give evidence about what you saw, observed or heard, so to say, not what assumption or conclusions or what "probably" had happened. So can you -- do you remember what happened and then to answer my questions, can you please do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I remember the nurses saying that they can't carry Martin, and that two soldiers came, and they carried him outside. But I didn't see the person issuing an order to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were there any -- you said two soldiers, what kind of soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Reservists.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When this took place, when you could see that in front of you, so to say, when these two reservists took up the stretcher in order to carry it away, were there any other soldiers in the -- nearby in that sequence, so to say, and not -- not just only that sequence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Not in the very room. Not in the room. There were no soldiers in the same room with the wounded, apart from the two soldiers, one of whom was calling out the names from the list, and there was another one standing beside him, plus the two who carried Martin out.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. And what were you doing? You said that Martin was carried out. Just briefly answer, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I took my bag, Tanja accompanied me, and we walked next to the stretcher and came out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And where did you go directly after that? You said that you went out of the room, and where did you go and Tanja go? Directly after that. And not any longer, just that sequence.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: We went outside, and we were searched by the soldiers. They searched the bag and us too. We -- told us to move on and then Tanja and I followed Martin, the stretcher and the two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: And we accompanied them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Were -- when you say that you went outside and you were searched by soldiers, what kind of soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've had that quite in detail before the break, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Were you -- were there other people around, or were there other that were searched by those soldiers, Mrs. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were other women and children and people leaving to the other side. As one comes out of the hospital, the women and children were told to go to the right, and the wounded to the left; that is, toward the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And you say -- when you say here that women and children to the right and the wounded to the left, that group that compiled the wounded, what kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Some of them could walk by themselves. They walked to the buses. And those who couldn't walk were carried on stretchers and then - how should I say it - they were left close to the street where the buses were. They would put down the stretchers on the concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Dosen, we will -- I will show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And for the Court, it is the exhibit number 170, and the ERN number is 00531260. I would also like the witness to look at that specific photograph. Just a moment, please. So that is -- we have to continue here to the ERN number 00531260, please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, do you have that photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And you told us that you walked out of the hospital. Can you show on this photograph where you did -- where you did came -- where -- from where you went out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Is there any technical possibilities for the witness to show that so we can see it here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She has a photographic copy of this exhibit, I believe. She could mark that, but that will not be easy for us to view here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can it be possible, Your Honour, for the witness to tell her testimony by showing on that photograph in her answers where specific events took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be possible. You will have to try.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, if she is encouraged to mark the photographic copy she has of the exhibit, it will be possible then for us to get some view of it. Just how good that will be, we will see.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, do you have that photograph now in front of you, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What does that show, what kind of building is that? Is that the hospital of Vukovar? Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And you mentioned here that you went out of the hospital and you were searched, and there were other women and children, and one group went to the right, another group went to the left. I just want you now to show on that photograph --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: -- where you went out from the hospital and where the searches were started. Just show us that, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: It was here. That's the exit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mark that with an A, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And you mentioned here that one group went to the right side, another group went to the left side. Can you mark that and write an arrow, what you meant by the right side that, group that went to the right side, will you please mark that as in B?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: Women and children went that way and the wounded the other. On both sides there were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And now we move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before the witness leaves that, the first arrow which you have to the right side, could you please put a B against the tip of that arrow, Mrs. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Letter B to mark the direction where the women and children went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please put a letter C against the arrow marking the direction of the group that went to the left side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And could you put the letter D, I think twice, against what you described as soldiers who were on either side of that group that went to the left side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Dosen, you went out of the hospital, and in what group were you walking? You have different options here, so to say. And just mention the letter, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The letter C.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And who else were in that group? What kind of people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: It was only wounded or were there other people that were not wounded, or was it only wounded in that group? Do you know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: I know it for a fact that there were only the wounded and the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what -- what happened after you were searched by the soldiers? Just directly after that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: After the search they allowed me and Tanja to accompany Martin. We went in the direction of the arrow towards the letter C, that is together with the wounded and to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned here, Mrs. Dosen, buses, to the buses. Can you show on the same photograph and take the letter E where the buses were located when you saw them.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: One of the buses was here. And the other one here. This was number three.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you please take up the photograph a bit with the help of the court officer? Can you take that once again, please, because I didn't see it properly. So we don't have it --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The first bus was here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Hang on.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: The second one here. The third one here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the third one --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: And the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please turn up the photograph a little bit more so we see the whole -- the down of that page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just push the page up a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mrs. Dosen, you have now marked four E. Can you please numbering the four E, in terms of the buses, bus number, so to say. Where were the bus standing when you saw it, when you're coming out from the direction C?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could put just E1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the number 1 on that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the next bus, number 2.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the third bus, number 3.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
